pattern: ich · du · er / sie / es · wir · ihr · sie · Sie
explain: Personal pronouns stand for people and things: ich (I), du (you), er (he), sie (she), es (it), wir (we), ihr (you, several friends), sie (they). For one 'you', choose: du for friends, family and children, Sie for adults you don't know well, like a teacher or a neighbour. Polite Sie always has a capital S.
compare_en: English has one 'you'; German picks du (friendly), ihr (friendly, several people) or Sie (polite, one or more). sie can mean 'she' or 'they', and Sie means polite 'you': the verb ending helps you tell them apart.
title: Personal pronouns: ich, du, Sie

pattern: verb stem + ending: ich -e · du -st · er / sie / es -t
explain: A German verb changes its ending to match the subject (who does it). Take the infinitive, e.g. wohnen, drop -en to get the stem wohn-, then add the ending: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt. If the stem ends in -s, -ß or -z, du only adds -t: du heißt. If it ends in -t or -d, add an extra e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.
compare_en: English only adds -s for he, she and it (he lives). German gives almost every person its own ending, so the ending tells you who is doing it.
title: Present tense: ich heiße, du heißt

pattern: W-word + VERB + subject + …?
explain: W-questions ask for information. They start with a question word: wer? (who), wie? (how), wo? (where), woher? (where from), was? (what). The verb comes straight after it, in position 2, and then the subject. To ask someone's name, German uses wie: Wie heißt du?
compare_en: English often needs 'do' (Where do you live?). German never does: the verb itself stands in position 2: Wo wohnst du? Careful: wer means 'who', not 'where'.
title: W-questions: wie, wer, wo, woher

pattern: ich bin · du bist · er / sie / es ist · wir sind · ihr seid · sie / Sie sind
explain: sein (to be) is the most important verb, and it is irregular, so learn its forms by heart. Use it to say who you are, where you are from, how old you are and what someone is like: Ich bin Priya. Ich bin 25 Jahre alt. For jobs, German uses no 'a': Jonas ist Student.
compare_en: Like 'to be', sein is irregular in English too (I am, you are, he is). But German drops the 'a' with jobs: Ich bin Student = I am a student.
title: sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist

pattern: wir -en · ihr -t · sie / Sie -en
explain: In the plural, wir, sie (they) and Sie (polite you) all use the infinitive form: wir wohnen, sie wohnen, Sie wohnen. Only ihr (you, several friends) is different: it takes -t, like er: ihr wohnt. After a stem ending in -t or -d, ihr adds -et: ihr arbeitet.
compare_en: In English, we, you and they share one form (we live, they live). German is the same for wir, sie and Sie, but ihr has its own -t ending: ihr wohnt.
title: Present tense: wir, ihr, sie

pattern: VERB + subject + …?
explain: A yes/no question starts with the verb, and the subject comes right after it: Kommst du aus Indien? Wohnt Lena in Köln? The answer begins with ja (yes) or nein (no). When you speak, your voice goes up at the end.
compare_en: English adds do/does (Do you come from India?) or turns 'is' around (Is he married?). German just puts the verb first, for every verb: Kommst du …? Ist er …? There is no 'do'.
title: Yes/no questions: Kommst du aus Indien?

pattern: position 1 + VERB (position 2) + …
explain: In a German statement the verb with the ending always stands in position 2. Position 1 is one block: often the subject, but it can also be a word like hier or a phrase like in Berlin. A block can have several words: Lena und Jonas is one position. If something else is in position 1, the subject goes right after the verb.
compare_en: English keeps the subject before the verb: Here I live. German keeps the verb in position 2, even if the subject then comes after it: Hier wohne ich.
title: The verb in position 2

pattern: ich habe · du hast · er / sie / es hat · wir haben · ihr habt · sie / Sie haben
explain: haben means 'to have'. It is almost regular, but du and er/sie/es lose the b: du hast, er hat. Use it for family, things and time: Ich habe zwei Brüder. Hast du Zeit? Some feelings also use haben: Ich habe Hunger (I'm hungry), Ich habe Durst (I'm thirsty).
compare_en: haben works like 'have' (I have a brother). But where English says 'I am hungry', German says Ich habe Hunger, literally 'I have hunger'.
title: haben: ich habe, du hast

pattern: der / ein (masculine) · die / eine (feminine) · das / ein (neuter) · die (plural)
explain: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). Use der/die/das (the) for something already known, and ein/eine (a) for something new: Das ist ein Hund. Der Hund ist klein. In the plural the article is always die, and there is no plural of ein. Learn every noun with its article.
compare_en: English has one 'the' and one 'a'. German has three genders, and they don't always follow meaning: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter.
title: der, die, das and ein, eine

pattern: mein / dein / sein / ihr + noun (endings like ein)
explain: Possessive words say whose something is: mein (my), dein (your), sein (his), ihr (her), unser (our), euer (your, several friends), ihr (their), Ihr (your, polite). They take the same endings as ein: mein Vater, meine Mutter, mein Kind, meine Eltern.
compare_en: As in English, the owner decides: Jonas → sein (his), Lena → ihr (her). But German also adds -e when the thing owned is feminine or plural: sein Bruder, seine Schwester.
title: mein, dein, sein, ihr

pattern: subject + verb + den / einen + masculine noun (the object)
explain: The object is the person or thing the action is done to: Ich trinke einen Kaffee. It is in the accusative case. Good news: only masculine nouns change: der → den, ein → einen. Feminine (die, eine), neuter (das, ein) and plural stay the same. Verbs like haben, essen, trinken, nehmen and bestellen take an object.
compare_en: English shows this only with pronouns (he → him). German shows it on the article: Der Salat ist gut (subject), but Ich esse den Salat (object).
title: Accusative: den, einen

pattern: ich möchte + object · ich möchte + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: möchte means 'would like'. It is the polite way to ask for things in a café or shop: Ich möchte einen Tee, bitte. ich and er/sie/es have the same form, möchte, with no -t. With a second verb, that verb goes to the end in the infinitive: Ich möchte bezahlen.
compare_en: Like 'would like', möchte is more polite than 'want'. But there is no 'to' before the second verb: Ich möchte bezahlen = I would like to pay.
title: möchten: Ich möchte einen Kaffee

pattern: kein + noun · nicht + verb, adjective or der/die/das/mein + noun
explain: Use kein for 'no' or 'not a' before a noun that would have ein or no article: Ich habe keinen Hund. Ich trinke keinen Kaffee. kein takes the same endings as ein, and keine in the plural. Use nicht for everything else: verbs, adjectives, and nouns with der/die/das or mein: Das Essen ist nicht gut. Das ist nicht mein Tee.
compare_en: English says 'not a', 'not any' or 'no': I don't have a dog. German simply uses kein: Ich habe keinen Hund. Never say nicht ein.
title: kein or nicht

pattern: der Tisch → die Tische · die Tür → die Türen · das Bild → die Bilder · das Sofa → die Sofas
explain: German has several plural endings, so learn each noun with its plural: der Tisch, die Tische. The plural article is always die. Rough guide: most feminine nouns add -(e)n; many masculine nouns add -e, sometimes with an umlaut (ä, ö, ü); short neuter nouns often add -er with an umlaut; words from other languages add -s; nouns ending in -er often stay the same.
compare_en: English nearly always adds -s (tables, rooms). In German -s is the rarest ending, mostly for borrowed words like Sofas and Fotos. Some nouns don't change at all, like 'sheep': das Zimmer → die Zimmer.
title: Noun plurals: -e, -en, -er, -s, umlaut

pattern: Es gibt + accusative (einen / eine / ein / –)
explain: es gibt means 'there is' or 'there are'. It never changes: es gibt for one thing and for many things. What follows is an object (accusative), so masculine nouns take einen or keinen: Es gibt einen Balkon. In a question the verb comes first: Gibt es hier einen Aufzug?
compare_en: English switches between 'there is' and 'there are'. German always says es gibt (literally 'it gives'), followed by the accusative.
title: es gibt + accusative

pattern: noun + sein + adjective (no ending)
explain: An adjective describes something: groß (big), klein (small), hell (bright), ruhig (quiet), teuer (expensive). After sein the adjective has no ending at all, whatever the gender or number: Der Balkon ist klein. Die Küche ist klein. Die Zimmer sind klein. You can add sehr (very), zu (too) or nicht (not) in front of it.
compare_en: Just like English: The room is big. The adjective only gets an ending when it stands before a noun (ein großes Zimmer), which you will learn later.
title: Adjectives after sein: Das Zimmer ist groß

pattern: subject + VERB (position 2) + … + PREFIX (at the end)
explain: Some verbs have a small front part, the prefix: auf-, an-, ein-, mit-, fern-. In a normal sentence the prefix splits off and goes to the very end: aufstehen → Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf. The main part stands in position 2 as usual. In the dictionary the verb is one word, and the prefix is stressed: AUFstehen.
compare_en: English has verbs like this too: get up, call up, come along. German just pushes the small part to the end of the sentence, even after a long middle: Ich rufe morgen um acht Uhr Lena an.
title: Separable verbs: Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf

pattern: um + clock time · am + day / part of the day · im + month / season · von … bis …
explain: Use um for clock times (um 8 Uhr), am for days and parts of the day (am Montag, am Abend, am Wochenende), and im for months and seasons (im Mai, im Winter). von … bis means 'from … to/until': von 9 bis 17 Uhr. One exception: in der Nacht (at night).
compare_en: English uses at, on and in (at 8, on Monday, in May), and German uses um, am and im the same way. But 'in the evening' is am Abend, and 'at the weekend' is am Wochenende.
title: Time: um, am, von … bis

pattern: Time / place + VERB + subject + rest
explain: You can start a sentence with a time (heute, am Montag, um 8 Uhr) instead of the subject. The verb must still stand in position 2, so the subject moves behind the verb: Ich arbeite am Montag → Am Montag arbeite ich. This is very common in German.
compare_en: English keeps the subject before the verb: On Monday I work. In German that order is wrong (Am Montag ich arbeite ✗). The verb stays second, and the subject comes third.
title: Inversion: Am Montag arbeite ich

pattern: only du and er / sie / es: a → ä · e → i · e → ie
explain: Some common verbs change their vowel, but only with du and er/sie/es: fahren → du fährst, er fährt; sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht; lesen → du liest, sie liest. All other forms are regular: ich fahre, wir fahren, ihr fahrt. Learn these verbs together with their er form.
compare_en: English has nothing like this in the present tense. A tip: if the er form changes, the du form changes in the same way, and the rest stays regular.
title: Stem-changing verbs: fahren → fährt, lesen → liest

pattern: verb + gern · verb + lieber · verb + am liebsten
explain: To say you like doing something, put gern after the verb: Ich tanze gern (I like dancing). lieber means 'prefer' and am liebsten means 'like best of all': Ich schwimme lieber. Am liebsten lese ich. nicht gern means 'don't like'. For things you like, use mögen instead: Ich mag Kaffee.
compare_en: English uses the verb 'like': I like swimming. German keeps the action verb and adds the little word gern: Ich schwimme gern, literally 'I swim gladly'.
title: gern, lieber, am liebsten

pattern: subject + kann / will (position 2) + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: können (can, be able to) and wollen (want to) are modal verbs. The modal verb stands in position 2, and the main verb goes to the very end in the infinitive: Ich kann gut schwimmen. Lena will ins Kino gehen. ich and er/sie/es have the same form with no ending: ich kann, er kann; ich will, sie will.
compare_en: German will means 'want to', not 'will': Ich will tanzen = I want to dance. And English keeps the two verbs together (I can swim well), while German splits them: Ich kann gut schwimmen.
title: können and wollen + infinitive at the end

pattern: ich → mich · du → dich · er → ihn · sie → sie · es → es · wir → uns · ihr → euch
explain: When a pronoun is the object (the person or thing the action is done to), some forms change: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns, ihr → euch. sie, es and Sie stay the same. For things, the pronoun follows the gender: der Computer → ihn, die Jacke → sie, das Handy → es.
compare_en: English does this for people: he → him, we → us. German does it for things too: die Jacke is sie, so 'I'll take it' is Ich nehme sie.
title: Accusative pronouns: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es

pattern: subject + verb + meinen / deinen / seinen / ihren + masculine noun
explain: Possessives (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr) take the same endings as ein. So as an object, only masculine nouns change: mein → meinen. Ich suche meinen Schlüssel. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same: meine Tasche, mein Handy, meine Schuhe.
compare_en: English 'my' never changes. In German the ending shows whether the noun is the subject or the object: Mein Schlüssel ist weg (subject), Ich suche meinen Schlüssel (object).
title: Possessives in the accusative: meinen, deinen

pattern: welcher / welche / welches …? – dieser / diese / dieses
explain: welch- asks 'which?' when you choose between things, and dies- means 'this' and points at one. Both take endings like der, die, das: der → -er, die → -e, das → -es, plural die → -e. As an object, masculine -er becomes -en, just like der → den: Welchen Computer kaufst du? – Diesen.
compare_en: English 'which' and 'this' never change. In German the ending matches the article: der Schuh → dieser Schuh, die Jacke → diese Jacke, das Handy → dieses Handy.
title: welcher? dieser

pattern: Sie: Gehen Sie …! · du: Geh …! · ihr: Geht …!
explain: The imperative gives instructions, directions and requests, and the verb comes first. Sie: the verb + Sie (Gehen Sie geradeaus!). du: take the du form and drop du and -st (du kommst → Komm!). ihr: the ihr form without ihr (ihr kommt → Kommt!). The change e → i stays (Nimm!), but a → ä does not (Fahr!). Add bitte to sound polite.
compare_en: English has one form for everyone: Go straight on! German has three, depending on who you are talking to, and the Sie form keeps its pronoun: Gehen Sie!
title: Imperative: Gehen Sie! Geh! Geht!

pattern: mit / zu / von / aus / bei / nach + dative: dem · der · dem · den
explain: After mit, zu, von, aus, bei and nach the noun is always in the dative case. The articles change: der → dem, das → dem, die → der, plural die → den. Short forms: zu dem → zum, zu der → zur, von dem → vom, bei dem → beim. Use nach for towns and countries (nach Berlin), but zu for people and places (zum Arzt, zur Post).
compare_en: English 'to' can be zu or nach: nach Berlin, but zum Bahnhof and zu Lena. And after mit the article always changes: mit dem Bus (by bus).
title: mit, zu, von, aus, bei, nach + dative

pattern: Wo? (place) · Woher? (from where) · Wohin? (to where)
explain: German has three question words for places. wo? asks where something is: Wo ist die Post? woher? asks where from: Woher kommst du? – Aus Indien. wohin? asks where to: Wohin fährst du? – Nach Köln. Verbs of movement like gehen and fahren go with wohin; sein and wohnen go with wo.
compare_en: English uses 'where' for all three. A tip: if the English question could end in 'to' or 'from' (Where are you going to? Where are you from?), use wohin or woher.
title: Wo? Woher? Wohin?

pattern: subject + muss (position 2) + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: müssen means 'must' or 'have to': something is necessary. Like all modal verbs it stands in position 2, and the main verb goes to the end in the infinitive: Ich muss zum Arzt gehen. ich and er/sie/es both say muss, with no ending. Careful: nicht müssen means 'don't have to': Du musst nicht kommen.
compare_en: English 'must not' means it is forbidden, but German muss nicht only means 'not necessary'. For 'must not', German uses darf nicht.
title: müssen

pattern: subject + darf (position 2) + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: dürfen means 'may' or 'be allowed to'. Use it to ask for permission or to give it: Darf ich hier sitzen? With nicht it means 'must not', so it is forbidden: Hier darf man nicht rauchen. ich and er/sie/es have no ending, and the singular has no umlaut: ich darf, er darf.
compare_en: Darf ich …? is like 'May I …?'. And darf nicht is English 'must not' (not allowed), while muss nicht only means 'don't have to'.
title: dürfen

pattern: position 1 + MODAL (position 2) + … middle … + INFINITIVE (end)
explain: With a modal verb (können, müssen, dürfen, wollen, möchten) a German sentence makes a frame, the verb bracket: the modal verb in position 2 and the infinitive at the very end. Everything else (time, object, place, nicht) goes in the middle. A separable verb stays in one piece at the end: Ich muss früh aufstehen.
compare_en: In English the two verbs stand together: I must take a tablet. In German they open and close the sentence like a bracket: Ich muss eine Tablette nehmen.
title: Modal verb sentences: the verb bracket

pattern: subject + haben (position 2) + … + Partizip II (end): ge- + stem + -t
explain: The Perfekt is the usual way to talk about the past when you speak or write a message. It has two parts: haben in position 2 and the Partizip II (past participle) at the end. For regular verbs the participle is ge- + stem + -t: kaufen → gekauft, arbeiten → gearbeitet. Verbs ending in -ieren have no ge-: studieren → studiert.
compare_en: English often uses the simple past (I bought a ticket yesterday), but German says Ich habe gestern ein Ticket gekauft, literally 'I have bought'. And the participle goes to the end, not next to haben.
title: Perfekt with haben: Ich habe gekauft

pattern: subject + sein (position 2) + … + Partizip II (end)
explain: Some verbs use sein instead of haben in the Perfekt. These are verbs of movement from one place to another (fahren, fliegen, gehen, kommen, reisen), a few verbs of change (aufstehen), and sein and bleiben themselves: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. Wir sind zu Hause geblieben. All other verbs take haben.
compare_en: English always uses 'have' (I have gone), so this is new. Think 'movement from A to B = sein': Ich bin geflogen (I flew), but Ich habe ein Ticket gebucht (I booked a ticket).
title: Perfekt with sein: Ich bin gefahren

pattern: ge- + stem (often with a new vowel) + -en
explain: Many common verbs are irregular: their Partizip II ends in -en, and the vowel often changes: trinken → getrunken, schreiben → geschrieben, finden → gefunden. Some keep their vowel: essen → gegessen, sehen → gesehen. There is no rule to guess them, so learn each verb with its participle.
compare_en: English has irregular verbs too, and some look alike: drink – drunk, trinken – getrunken; find – found, finden – gefunden.
title: Irregular Partizip II: gegessen, getrunken

pattern: am + ordinal + -en (am ersten Mai) · im + month (im Juli)
explain: Dates use ordinal numbers (first, second …). Up to 19 add -te (zweite, vierte), from 20 add -ste (zwanzigste); erste, dritte, siebte and achte are special. 'On' a date is am + ordinal + -en: am ersten Mai. In writing a dot shows the ordinal: am 3. Oktober (say am dritten). For a whole month use im: im Juli.
compare_en: English writes 1st, 2nd, 3rd; German writes 1., 2., 3. and says am ersten, am zweiten, am dritten. 'In July' is im Juli, and 'today is the first' is Heute ist der erste.
title: Dates: am ersten Mai, im Juli

pattern: Es + weather verb (Es regnet.) · Es ist + adjective (Es ist kalt.)
explain: For the weather German always uses es as the subject, like English 'it': Es regnet (it's raining). Es ist kalt. Es ist warm. Because es is the subject, the verb takes the er/sie/es form. In a question or after a time phrase, es comes right after the verb: Regnet es? Im Winter ist es kalt.
compare_en: Like English 'it is raining', but German has no -ing: Es regnet means both 'it rains' and 'it's raining'. Never drop es: Heute ist kalt ✗ → Heute ist es kalt ✓.
title: es: Es regnet, es ist kalt

pattern: prefix + ge + participle: einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen
explain: In the Perfekt of a separable verb, ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen, einladen → eingeladen. The participle is one word, at the end. Movement and change verbs still take sein: Ich bin um 7 Uhr aufgestanden. Der Zug ist pünktlich angekommen.
compare_en: English keeps the small word separate (I called him up). German glues it to the front of the participle, with ge- in the middle: Ich habe ihn angerufen.
title: Perfekt of separable verbs: eingekauft

pattern: subject + haben/sein (position 2) + … + Partizip II (at the end)
explain: The Perfekt is the usual way to talk about the past when you speak. haben or sein stands in position 2, and the Partizip II (past participle: gewohnt, gefahren) goes to the end. Most verbs take haben. Take sein for movement from A to B (fahren, fliegen, umziehen), for a change of state (aufwachen, werden), and for sein and bleiben.
compare_en: English always uses "have" (I have gone), but German says ich bin gegangen for movement. German also uses the Perfekt where English uses the simple past: Ich habe in Köln gewohnt = I lived in Cologne.
title: Perfekt review: haben or sein?

pattern: subject + werden + job / adjective / age
explain: werden means "to become" or "to get". Use it for jobs (Ich werde Ärztin, with no article before the job), for changes (Es wird kalt) and for birthdays (Lena wird 30). It is irregular: du wirst, er/sie wird. In the Perfekt it takes sein: Er ist Arzt geworden.
compare_en: English uses "become", "get" or "turn": it's getting cold = es wird kalt, she turns 30 = sie wird 30. False friend: bekommen means "to get, to receive", never "to become".
title: werden as a full verb: Ich werde Ärztin

pattern: main clause + , aber / denn / sondern + subject + VERB + … (normal order)
explain: und (and), aber (but), oder (or), denn (because) and sondern (but rather) join two main clauses without changing the word order. They sit in "position 0", so the subject and the verb follow as usual. Use sondern only after a negative (nicht, kein) to give the correct thing. Put a comma before aber, denn and sondern.
compare_en: English uses "but" for both aber and sondern; German keeps sondern for correcting a negative: nicht Tee, sondern Kaffee = not tea but coffee. denn means "because" and keeps the normal word order.
title: und, aber, oder, denn, sondern

pattern: Wo? → in / an / auf … + dative · Wohin? → in / an / auf … + accusative
explain: Nine prepositions can take two cases: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen. If you say where something is (Wo?), use the dative (dem, der, dem, den). If something moves to a new place (Wohin?), use the accusative (den, die, das, die). Short forms: in dem → im, an dem → am, in das → ins, an das → ans.
compare_en: English sometimes shows this with "in" and "into" or "on" and "onto". German shows it with the article: im Garten (in the garden), in den Garten (into the garden).
title: Two-way prepositions: Wo? dative, Wohin? accusative

pattern: stellen / legen / hängen + Wohin? + accusative · stehen / liegen / hängen + Wo? + dative
explain: These verbs come in pairs. stellen (put upright), legen (lay down) and hängen (hang up) are actions: you move something, so the place takes the accusative (Wohin?). stehen (stand), liegen (lie) and hängen (be hanging) say where something is, so the place takes the dative (Wo?). Perfekt: hat gestellt, hat gelegt, but hat gestanden, hat gelegen.
compare_en: English often just says "put" and "is". German picks the verb by position: upright things stand (die Flasche steht), flat things lie (das Handy liegt). Plates and shoes usually "stand" in German.
title: stellen/stehen, legen/liegen, hängen

pattern: dem (masc. / neut.) · der (fem.) · den + noun-n (plural)
explain: The dative is the case for the person who receives something and for the noun after mit, bei, von, zu, aus, nach and seit. The articles change: der and das → dem, die → der, plural die → den, and the plural noun adds -n (den Kindern). ein, kein and mein follow the same pattern: einem, einer, meinen.
compare_en: English shows this only in pronouns (he → him); German shows it on the article too: der Mann → mit dem Mann (with the man).
title: Dative articles: dem, der, den

pattern: main clause + , weil + subject + … + VERB (at the end)
explain: weil means "because". It starts a subordinate clause (a part of a sentence that can't stand alone), and the conjugated verb (the one with the personal ending) goes to the very end. A separable verb joins up again: …, weil ich früh aufstehe. With a modal verb, the modal comes last: …, weil ich arbeiten muss. Put a comma before weil.
compare_en: In English the word order after "because" stays the same; in German the verb jumps to the end: because I am ill = weil ich krank bin.
title: weil: the verb goes to the end

pattern: Ich glaube / weiß / finde / hoffe, + dass + subject + … + VERB (at the end)
explain: dass means "that". It introduces what someone thinks, knows, says or hopes, after verbs like glauben, denken, wissen, finden, hoffen and sagen. Like weil, it starts a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end. Put a comma before dass.
compare_en: English can drop "that" (I think he's right); German keeps dass, or drops it and uses normal order: Ich glaube, er hat recht. Don't mix up dass (that, joining two clauses) and das (the / that thing).
title: dass: Ich glaube, dass …

pattern: sentence 1 + , deshalb + VERB + subject + …
explain: deshalb means "that's why" or "so": it introduces the result of what came before. deshalb takes position 1, like the time word in Am Montag arbeite ich, so the verb comes straight after it and the subject follows. darum and deswegen mean the same and work the same way.
compare_en: In English the subject comes right after "so" (so I'm staying at home); in German the verb comes first: deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause. weil gives the reason, deshalb gives the result.
title: deshalb: the verb comes right after

pattern: subject + verb + reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch) + …
explain: Reflexive verbs come with a reflexive pronoun, a small word that points back to the subject: ich freue mich, du freust dich. The pronoun is part of the verb, even when English has nothing there. The forms are like mich, dich, uns, euch, but er, sie, es and Sie all take sich. In the plural it can mean "each other": Wir treffen uns.
compare_en: English sometimes says -self (I wash myself) but often nothing: I'm looking forward = ich freue mich, we meet = wir treffen uns, I'm getting dressed = ich ziehe mich an.
title: Reflexive verbs: sich freuen, sich treffen

pattern: verb + fixed preposition + case: warten auf + accusative
explain: Many verbs go with a fixed preposition, and the preposition decides the case. You can't work it out from English, so learn the verb, the preposition and the case together: warten auf (+ acc.), sich interessieren für (+ acc.), sich freuen auf (+ acc.) for something coming and über (+ acc.) for something already here, denken an (+ acc.), sprechen mit (+ dat.), Angst haben vor (+ dat.).
compare_en: English has fixed prepositions too, but they rarely match: warten auf = wait for (not "on"), sich interessieren für = be interested in, Angst vor = afraid of.
title: Verbs with prepositions: warten auf, sich interessieren für

pattern: wo(r) + preposition? → question · da(r) + preposition → "it / that"
explain: With verbs that take a preposition, ask about a thing with wo + preposition (Worauf wartest du?) and refer back to a thing with da + preposition (Ich warte darauf). Add -r- if the preposition starts with a vowel: wo-r-über, da-r-auf. For people, keep the preposition with wen/wem or a pronoun: Auf wen wartest du? – Auf ihn.
compare_en: English leaves the preposition at the end or adds "it": What are you waiting for? – I'm waiting for it. German joins the preposition to wo- or da-: Worauf? – Darauf.
title: worauf? darauf: questions and pronouns

pattern: der / die / das + adjective-e or -en + noun
explain: Before a noun, an adjective takes an ending. After der, die, das (and dieser, welcher, jeder) the article already shows the case, so the adjective only needs -e or -en. It's -e after der, die, das in the nominative (the subject) and after die, das in the accusative (the object). Everywhere else it's -en: den (masc. accusative), the whole dative and all plurals.
compare_en: English adjectives never change (the red jacket, with the red jacket); German adjectives before a noun always take an ending. After sein there is no ending: Die Jacke ist rot.
title: Adjective endings after der, die, das

pattern: ein / kein / mein + adjective-er, -e, -es or -en + noun
explain: ein has no ending in three places: masculine nominative (ein Mantel) and neuter nominative and accusative (ein Kleid). There the adjective shows the gender instead: ein neuer Mantel, ein neues Kleid. Everywhere else the endings are the same as after der, die, das: eine neue Jacke, einen neuen Mantel, mit einem neuen Kleid, meine neuen Schuhe.
compare_en: In English it is always "a new coat, my new coat". In German the adjective carries the gender that ein can't show: ein neuer Rock (der), ein neues Hemd (das).
title: Adjective endings after ein, kein, mein

pattern: adjective + the article's ending (-er, -e, -es, -em, -en) + noun
explain: With no article in front, the adjective does the article's job and takes its ending: der → -er, die → -e, das → -es, dem → -em, den → -en. You meet this with plurals (bunte T-Shirts), things you don't count (frisches Brot, kalte Milch) and set phrases (Liebe Grüße, Mit freundlichen Grüßen).
compare_en: English just drops the article (fresh bread, cold milk). In German the article's ending moves onto the adjective: frisches Brot (das Brot), kalte Milch (die Milch).
title: Adjective endings with no article

pattern: Wenn + subject + … + VERB, + VERB + subject + …
explain: wenn means "if" (a condition) and also "when" or "whenever" (every time something happens). It starts a subordinate clause, so its verb goes to the end. If the wenn-clause comes first, it counts as position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb: Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich. The two verbs meet at the comma.
compare_en: English keeps subject + verb in both halves: If I have time, I'll come. German puts the two verbs side by side: … Zeit habe, komme ich. Don't confuse wenn with wann, the question word "when?".
title: wenn: if and whenever

pattern: subject + sollte(n) + … + infinitive · An deiner Stelle würde ich + … + infinitive
explain: To give friendly advice, use sollte (a form of sollen) with an infinitive at the end: Du solltest mehr schlafen. It is softer than musst. Another way is An deiner Stelle würde ich … (If I were you, I would …), again with the infinitive at the end. Both are Konjunktiv II forms, the German "would / should" mood.
compare_en: sollte = "should", würde = "would", and both send the second verb to the end: You should drink more water = Du solltest mehr Wasser trinken.
title: Advice: Du solltest …, An deiner Stelle würde ich …

pattern: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen / Ihnen (dative)
explain: Dative pronouns answer "to whom?" or "for whom?". You need them after verbs like helfen, gefallen and schmecken, after dative prepositions (mit mir, bei dir), and in set phrases: Wie geht es dir? Mir ist kalt. Pain works the same way: Mir tut der Kopf weh (literally: to me the head hurts).
compare_en: English uses one object form for both cases (me, him, her); German has a separate dative: Er sieht mich (he sees me), but Er hilft mir (he helps me).
title: Dative pronouns: mir, dir, ihm, ihr

pattern: ich war, du warst, er war … · ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte …
explain: For sein and haben, Germans normally use the Präteritum (the simple past) instead of the Perfekt, even when speaking: Ich war in Wien sounds more natural than Ich bin in Wien gewesen. The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same (war, hatte), and the other endings look like the present: du warst, wir waren, ihr wart.
compare_en: war = was / were, hatte = had. English uses the simple past here too (I was tired, we had no time), so this one feels familiar.
title: Präteritum: war, hatte

pattern: subject + konnte / musste / wollte / durfte + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen) also use the Präteritum for the past. Drop the umlaut and add -te to the stem: können → konnte, müssen → musste, dürfen → durfte, wollen → wollte, sollen → sollte. The ich and er/sie forms are the same. The second verb stays at the end as an infinitive.
compare_en: konnte = could / was able to, musste = had to, wollte = wanted to, durfte = was allowed to. Careful: ich will means "I want to", not "I will".

en: at the airport for two hours.

title: Präteritum of modals: konnte, musste, wollte

pattern: Wo? in den Bergen / am Meer / auf dem Land · Wohin? in die Berge / ans Meer / aufs Land
explain: Holiday places follow the two-way rule: dative for where you are (Wo?), accusative for where you go (Wohin?). Choose the preposition by the type of place: in for mountains and for countries with an article (in die Schweiz), an for the sea, a lake or the coast (am Meer, an die Ostsee), auf for islands and the countryside (auf dem Land). Cities: in Berlin, but nach Berlin.
compare_en: English says "at the seaside", "in the mountains", "to the coast". German picks in, an or auf by the type of place, then the case by Wo? or Wohin?.
title: Places: in den Bergen, am Meer, an die Ostsee

pattern: Wissen Sie / Können Sie mir sagen, + W-word + subject + … + VERB (at the end)?
explain: To ask more politely, put a W-question (wo, wann, wie, was, warum …) inside a frame like Wissen Sie, …? or Können Sie mir sagen, …? The W-word then starts a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: Wo ist der Bahnhof? → Wissen Sie, wo der Bahnhof ist? After Ich weiß nicht, … the sentence ends with a full stop.
compare_en: English does the same: "Where is the station?" becomes "Do you know where the station is?". In German the verb goes all the way to the end.
title: Indirect questions: Wissen Sie, wo …?

pattern: Ich weiß nicht / Weißt du, + ob + subject + … + VERB (at the end)
explain: ob means "whether" or "if". Use it to turn a yes/no question (one with no W-word) into an indirect question: Kommt er? → Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. Like dass and weil, ob sends the verb to the end. For a W-question, keep the W-word instead: Ich weiß nicht, wann er kommt.
compare_en: English says "if" or "whether" here: I don't know if he's coming. In German, "if" as a condition is wenn, but "if" meaning "whether" is always ob.
title: ob: Ich weiß nicht, ob …

pattern: sentence 1 + , trotzdem + VERB + subject + …
explain: trotzdem means "still", "anyway" or "nevertheless": something happens although you would expect the opposite. Like deshalb, it can take position 1, so the verb comes straight after it and then the subject. It can also stand after the verb: Ich gehe trotzdem.
compare_en: English usually puts "still" or "anyway" in the middle or at the end (but I still went); German often starts with trotzdem and puts the verb straight after it: trotzdem bin ich gegangen.
title: trotzdem: still, nevertheless

pattern: subject + helfen / danken / gratulieren / gefallen / gehören / schmecken + dative
explain: A few common verbs take a dative object instead of an accusative: helfen, danken, gratulieren, antworten, gefallen, gehören, schmecken, passen. Learn them as a group. With gefallen, gehören and schmecken the thing is the subject and the person is in the dative: Das Kleid gefällt mir (literally: the dress pleases me).
compare_en: In English these verbs take a normal object (help him, thank you). In German it's the dative: ich helfe ihm, ich danke dir. "I like the dress" is turned around: Das Kleid gefällt mir.
title: Verbs with the dative: helfen, gefallen, gehören

pattern: subject + verb + dative (person) + accusative (thing) · pronoun thing first: Ich gebe es dir.
explain: Verbs like geben, schenken, schicken, zeigen, bringen and erklären can have two objects: a person in the dative (who gets it) and a thing in the accusative (what). The usual order is person before thing: Ich schenke meiner Mutter eine Tasche. But when the thing is a pronoun (es, ihn, sie), it comes first: Ich schenke sie ihr.
compare_en: English uses the same order (I give my mother a bag) or adds "to" (I give it to her). German needs no "to": the dative does that job. With two pronouns, "it" comes first in both: Ich gebe es dir = I give it to you.
title: Two objects: Ich schenke dir ein Buch

pattern: name + -s + noun (no apostrophe): Lenas Geburtstag
explain: To say whose something is, add -s to the name and put it in front of the noun: Lenas Geburtstag (Lena's birthday). Write no apostrophe and no article. Names that already end in -s, -ß, -x or -z get only an apostrophe: Jonas' Party. In everyday speech you can also use von: der Geburtstag von Lena.
compare_en: It's just like English 's, but without the apostrophe: Priyas Familie = Priya's family. For names ending in -s, German writes only the apostrophe: Jonas' Freund.
title: Names with -s: Lenas Geburtstag

pattern: adjective-er + als · so + adjective + wie
explain: To compare two things, add -er to the adjective and use als (than): Berlin ist größer als Köln. Many short adjectives also get an umlaut: alt → älter, groß → größer, jung → jünger. A few are irregular: gut → besser, viel → mehr, gern → lieber. To say two things are equal, use so … wie: Lena ist so alt wie Jonas.
compare_en: English adds -er or uses "more" (more interesting); German always adds -er, even to long words: interessanter. "than" is als (not dann), and "as … as" is so … wie.
title: Comparative: größer als, so groß wie

pattern: am + adjective-sten (after a verb) · der / die / das + adjective-ste + noun
explain: The superlative says something is "the most". After a verb use am …sten: Dieser Kurs ist am besten. Before a noun use the article + …ste with the normal ending: der beste Kurs, die schönste Stadt. After -t, -d, -s, -ß or -z you usually add -esten (am ältesten, am kürzesten), but groß → am größten. Irregular: gut → am besten, viel → am meisten, gern → am liebsten.
compare_en: English uses -est or "most" (the most interesting); German always adds -st: am interessantesten. am …sten is simply "the …est" after a verb: Dieses Fach ist am schwersten = this subject is the hardest.
title: Superlative: am größten, der größte

pattern: Perfekt for most verbs · Präteritum for sein, haben, es gibt and the modal verbs
explain: When you tell a story in speech, mix the two past tenses. Use the Perfekt for most verbs (Ich habe Englisch gelernt), but the Präteritum (simple past) for sein, haben and the modal verbs (Ich war zehn, ich hatte einen tollen Lehrer, ich musste viel lernen). es gibt also goes into the Präteritum: es gab (there was / there were).
compare_en: English uses the simple past for everything (I was, I had, I learned). German speech uses the Perfekt for most verbs, so "I learned" becomes ich habe gelernt, but "I was" stays ich war.
title: Talking about the past: war, hatte, konnte

pattern: Könnten / Würden Sie + … + infinitive (at the end)?
explain: For polite requests, use könnten (could) or würden (would) instead of können: Könnten Sie mir helfen? sounds friendlier than Können Sie mir helfen? The second verb goes to the end as an infinitive, and bitte makes it even more polite. These are Konjunktiv II forms, the German "could / would" mood.
compare_en: Just like English: "Can you …?" becomes "Could you …?" or "Would you …?". könnten = could, würden = would.
title: Polite requests: Könnten Sie …? Würden Sie …?

pattern: Ich hätte gern + accusative (a thing)
explain: Ich hätte gern … (I'd like …) is the polite way to ask for something in a shop, café or office. hätte is the Konjunktiv II (would-form) of haben, and the thing you want is in the accusative: Ich hätte gern einen Termin. It is used like möchte, but only with a thing, never with a second verb.
compare_en: It matches English "I'd like …" or "I'll have …". Avoid Ich will …: it sounds like "I want", which is too direct in a shop.
title: Ich hätte gern …

pattern: subject + lassen + object + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: lassen + infinitive means you get someone else to do a job for you: Ich lasse mein Fahrrad reparieren (a mechanic repairs it). lassen is the conjugated verb in position 2, and the second verb goes to the end. Watch the vowel: du lässt, er/sie lässt, but ihr lasst.
compare_en: English says "have / get something done" with a past participle: I'm having my bike repaired. German uses the infinitive instead: reparieren, not repariert.
title: lassen: Ich lasse das Fahrrad reparieren

pattern: verb / expression + , + … + zu + infinitive (at the end)
explain: After some verbs and expressions the second verb goes to the end with zu: versuchen, vergessen, anfangen, Lust haben, Zeit haben, es ist wichtig / schön. Put a comma before the zu-part. With separable verbs zu goes in the middle: auszumachen, aufzustehen. After modal verbs (können, müssen, sollen …) there is no zu.
compare_en: zu + infinitive is like English "to + verb": I'm trying to drive less = Ich versuche, weniger Auto zu fahren, but the zu-part goes to the end. As in English, modal verbs take no "to": I must go = Ich muss gehen.
title: zu + infinitive: Ich versuche, weniger zu fahren

pattern: reason → deshalb + VERB + subject … · obstacle → trotzdem + VERB + subject …
explain: Both words take position 1, so the verb follows straight after them, then the subject. Choose by meaning: deshalb (so, that's why) brings the result you would expect; trotzdem (but … still, anyway) brings a result you would not expect. Es regnet, deshalb nehme ich den Bus. Es regnet, trotzdem fahre ich mit dem Fahrrad.
compare_en: deshalb = so / that's why, trotzdem = but … still / anyway. In English the subject comes first after both; in German the verb does.
title: deshalb or trotzdem?

pattern: man + verb in the er/sie/es form + …
explain: man means "people in general", "you" or "one". It takes the same verb form as er/sie/es: man kann, man sollte, man fährt. Use it for rules, advice and what people usually do. man is always the subject and has one n; der Mann (the man) has two.
compare_en: English uses "you", "people" or "one": How do you say that? = Wie sagt man das? In Germany people cycle a lot = In Deutschland fährt man viel Fahrrad.
title: man: Man sollte Müll trennen

pattern: noun, + der / die / das / den (relative pronoun) + … + verb (at the end)
explain: A relative clause describes a noun, like English 'who', 'which' or 'that'. It starts with a relative pronoun: its gender and number come from the noun it describes, but its case comes from its job inside the clause. As the subject it is nominative (der, die, das, die); as the object it is accusative, and only the masculine changes: der → den. A comma opens the clause and the conjugated verb goes to the end.
compare_en: English chooses between who and whom, or leaves the pronoun out ('the man I know'). German never drops it: der Mann, den ich kenne.
title: Relative clauses: der Mann, der / den …

pattern: noun, + dem / der / denen (dative relative pronoun) + … + verb (at the end)
explain: When the noun has a dative job inside the relative clause, the relative pronoun is dative: dem (masculine and neuter), der (feminine), denen (plural). This happens after verbs that take the dative, such as helfen, gefallen, gehören, schmecken and danken, and for the person you give or explain something to. Watch the plural: denen, which is longer than the article den. The verb still goes to the end.
compare_en: English uses whom or 'to whom' here, or moves 'to' to the end: die Frau, der ich helfe = the woman (whom) I help; der Kollege, dem das Auto gehört = the colleague the car belongs to.
title: Relative clauses in the dative: dem, der, denen

pattern: noun, + preposition + relative pronoun (case set by the preposition) + … + verb (at the end)
explain: If the verb in the relative clause needs a preposition (sprechen mit, sich freuen auf, suchen nach), the preposition comes first, straight after the comma, and the relative pronoun follows it. The preposition decides the case: mit and nach take the dative (mit dem, mit der, mit denen); für takes the accusative, and so does auf in sich freuen auf (für den, auf die). Gender and number still come from the noun.
compare_en: English usually moves the preposition to the end: 'the friend I live with'. German never does: der Freund, mit dem ich wohne. The preposition stays in front of the pronoun.
title: Relative clauses with prepositions: mit dem, über die

pattern: subject + werden (conjugated) + … + Partizip II (at the end)
explain: The passive puts the action in focus, not the person doing it: what happens to something. Form it with werden (wird, werden …) plus the Partizip II (the past participle, e.g. geliefert) at the end of the clause. To say who does it, add von + dative: von der Chefin. It is common for processes at work, rules and instructions.
compare_en: English builds the passive with 'be' (is delivered); German uses werden (wird geliefert). Careful: Das Paket ist geliefert describes a finished state (it has been delivered), not the action.
title: Passive: Das Paket wird geliefert

pattern: subject + wurde / wurden + … + Partizip II (at the end)
explain: To say what was done in the past, put werden into the Präteritum (simple past): wurde (singular), wurden (plural), with the Partizip II at the end. This is the usual past passive in reports and texts. In the Perfekt it is ist … worden: Das Haus ist 1990 gebaut worden (worden, not geworden).
compare_en: English 'was built' = German wurde gebaut. Don't mix up wurde (was, past passive) with würde (would): the umlaut changes the meaning.
title: Passive in the past: wurde gebaut

pattern: subject + modal verb (conjugated) + … + Partizip II + werden (at the end)
explain: To say what must, can or should be done, combine a modal verb with the passive. The modal (muss, kann, soll, darf) takes position 2, and the end of the clause holds the Partizip II followed by werden: muss gemacht werden. In a subordinate clause (one starting with dass, weil …) the modal moves to the very end: …, dass der Bericht heute geschrieben werden muss.
compare_en: It matches English 'must be done': modal + be + participle. German puts the last two in the opposite order: gemacht werden = be done.
title: Passive with modals: muss gemacht werden

pattern: regular: stem + -te (lernte) · irregular: new stem (ging, kam, fand) + endings · ich and er/sie/es: no ending
explain: The Präteritum (simple past) is the past tense of written German: stories, reports, CVs and the news. In speech Germans mostly use the Perfekt, except with sein, haben and the modal verbs. Regular verbs add -te to the stem (lernen → lernte). Irregular verbs change their vowel (gehen → ging, finden → fand) and must be learned. The ich and er/sie/es forms have no ending: ich ging, sie ging.
compare_en: It works like English: regular verbs add an ending (learned = lernte), irregular ones change the vowel (go → went, find → found = gehen → ging, finden → fand). Many verbs are irregular in both languages.
title: Präteritum of all verbs: ging, kam, fand

pattern: mixed verbs: new stem + regular -te endings (denken → dachte, bringen → brachte, wissen → wusste)
explain: A small group of 'mixed' verbs changes its stem like irregular verbs but takes the regular -te endings. The important ones: denken → dachte, bringen → brachte, wissen → wusste, kennen → kannte, nennen → nannte, rennen → rannte. Their Partizip II is mixed too: gedacht, gebracht, gewusst, gekannt. Never say denkte or bringte.
compare_en: English has the same type of verb: think → thought, bring → brought. They match closely: dachte = thought, brachte = brought.
title: Mixed verbs: dachte, brachte, wusste

pattern: main clause, + seit(dem) / bis + subject + … + verb (at the end)
explain: seit (or seitdem) and bis can also join two clauses, and then they send the verb to the end. seit(dem) = since: something started in the past and is still true, so German uses the present tense. bis = until: something lasts up to a point. You know both as prepositions (seit einem Jahr, bis Montag); as conjunctions they are followed by a whole clause with its own verb.
compare_en: English since and until work the same way, but where English says 'Since I have lived here', German uses the present: Seit ich hier wohne …
title: seit and bis as conjunctions

pattern: Ich wäre / hätte / würde gern … · Wenn + subject + doch / nur + … + wäre / hätte (at the end)!
explain: To say what you would like, use the Konjunktiv II, the 'would' form of the verb: Ich wäre gern fitter (would be), Ich hätte gern mehr Zeit (would have). With most other verbs use würde + infinitive: Ich würde gern Tennis spielen. A strong wish about something that isn't true starts with Wenn, adds doch or nur, and puts the verb at the end: Wenn ich doch gesund wäre!
compare_en: English says 'I'd like to be …' or 'If only I had …'. German: Ich wäre gern … and Wenn ich nur … hätte! wäre = would be, hätte = would have, würde = would.
title: Wishes: Ich wäre gern …, Wenn ich doch …

pattern: Wenn + subject + … + Konjunktiv II (at the end), + würde / wäre / hätte + subject + … (+ infinitive)
explain: To talk about something that is only imagined, not real now, use the Konjunktiv II in both parts. In the wenn clause the verb goes to the end: Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, … The main clause then starts with its verb: … würde ich jeden Tag joggen. Use wäre, hätte, könnte and müsste for sein, haben, können and müssen, and würde + infinitive for most other verbs.
compare_en: English uses the past in the if-part and 'would' in the other: If I had time, I would go. German uses the Konjunktiv II in both parts: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich gehen.
title: Unreal conditions: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich …

pattern: hätte / wäre + … + Partizip II (at the end)
explain: To talk about how the past could have been (but wasn't), use hätte or wäre plus the Partizip II. Choose them as in the Perfekt: verbs that take haben use hätte (hätte gelernt), verbs of movement or change that take sein use wäre (wäre gegangen). It is the form for regrets and missed chances: Wenn ich mich aufgewärmt hätte, hätte ich mich nicht verletzt.
compare_en: This is English 'would have done' and 'if I had done': hätte gemacht = would have done / had done, wäre gekommen = would have come / had come.
table: I would have trained / had trained
I would have run / had run
title: Konjunktiv II in the past: hätte gemacht

pattern: main clause, + obwohl + subject + … + verb (at the end)
explain: obwohl means although: it adds a fact that you would expect to stop the main action, but it doesn't. obwohl is a subordinating conjunction (a joining word that starts a side clause), so the conjugated verb goes to the very end of its clause. If the obwohl clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb: Obwohl es spät war, sah Jonas noch fern.
compare_en: obwohl = although / even though, used in the same way. Only the word order differs: the verb waits until the end.
title: obwohl: although

pattern: …, obwohl + … + verb (at the end) · …. Trotzdem + verb + subject + …
explain: Both express a contrast, but they work differently. obwohl starts a side clause and sends the verb to the end: Ich gehe, obwohl ich müde bin. trotzdem is an adverb meaning 'anyway, still': it points back to the sentence before, and when it takes position 1 the verb comes straight after it: Ich bin müde. Trotzdem gehe ich. obwohl goes with the reason against; trotzdem goes with what happens anyway.
compare_en: obwohl = although; trotzdem = anyway / still / nevertheless. 'I'm tired, but I'm going anyway' = Ich bin müde, aber ich gehe trotzdem.
table: at the end of its clause
title: obwohl or trotzdem?

pattern: Er sagt, er sei / habe / komme … (Konjunktiv I: stem + -e for er / sie / es)
explain: News reports use the Konjunktiv I to repeat what someone said without confirming it: Der Minister sagt, er sei zufrieden. At B1 you only need to recognise it. The forms you will meet are er/sie/es + stem + -e: sei (is), habe (has), komme (comes), müsse (must), könne (can), werde (will). In everyday speech people use dass or the normal present instead: Er sagt, dass er krank ist.
compare_en: English has no special form; it simply reports: 'He says he is ill.' In German news, sei and habe signal 'this is what he said', a reported claim, not a fact the writer confirms.
title: Indirect speech: Er sagt, er sei krank (recognition)

pattern: noun + des / eines …(e)s (masculine, neuter) · der / einer … (feminine, plural)
explain: The genitive shows that something belongs to someone or something: das Auto des Lehrers, the teacher's car. It comes after the noun it describes. Masculine and neuter use des / eines and add -s or -es to the noun (des Mannes, des Geschäfts); feminine and plural use der / einer and the noun doesn't change. In speech people often say von + dative instead, but you need the genitive for reading and writing.
compare_en: It works like English 's or 'of': der Preis des Handys = the price of the phone. Like 'of', it follows the noun; only names go in front: Lenas Fahrrad = Lena's bike.
title: The genitive: des Mannes, der Frau

pattern: wegen / trotz / während + genitive (des …(e)s / der …)
explain: A few prepositions take the genitive. The most common are wegen (because of), trotz (despite) and während (during). They give a reason, a contrast or a time in one short phrase instead of a whole clause: wegen des Regens = weil es regnet. In speech you will often hear wegen dem Regen (dative), but in writing and in the exam use the genitive.
compare_en: wegen = because of, trotz = despite / in spite of, während = during. The clause versions are weil (because), obwohl (although) and während (while).
title: wegen, trotz, während + genitive

pattern: des / der / eines / einer + adjective-en + noun (the ending is -en)
explain: In the genitive, an adjective after an article or a possessive (mein, unser …) always ends in -en: des neuen Handys, der alten Kundin, eines guten Freundes, meiner neuen Schuhe. Masculine and neuter nouns still add their -s. Only with no article at all do feminine and plural adjectives take -er (trotz großer Mühe), which is rare at B1.
compare_en: English adjectives never change. In the German genitive the rule is simple: after an article the adjective ends in -en.
title: Adjective endings in the genitive

pattern: hatte / war (Präteritum) + … + Partizip II (at the end)
explain: The Plusquamperfekt (past perfect) shows that one past event happened before another past event. Form it like the Perfekt, but put haben or sein into the Präteritum: hatte gebucht, war gefahren. Verbs that take sein in the Perfekt (movement, change of state) take war; all others take hatte. It often appears together with nachdem.
compare_en: It is the English past perfect: hatte gebucht = had booked, war abgefahren = had left. English uses 'had' for both; German chooses hatte or war.
title: Plusquamperfekt: hatte gemacht, war gefahren

pattern: Nachdem + subject + … + Partizip II + hatte / war (at the end), + verb + subject + …
explain: nachdem means after (+ a clause): first one thing happened, then another. It starts a side clause, so its verb goes to the end. The nachdem clause is one tense earlier than the main clause: Plusquamperfekt (hatte/war + Partizip II) when the main clause is in the past, Perfekt when the main clause is in the present.
compare_en: Like English 'after' + clause, with the past perfect for the earlier action: Nachdem ich gegessen hatte … = After I had eaten …. Before a noun German uses nach instead: nach dem Essen.
title: nachdem

pattern: Bevor + subject + … + verb (at the end), + verb + subject + …
explain: bevor means before (+ a clause): the main clause happens first, and the bevor clause names what comes later. It sends the verb to the end. Unlike nachdem, both clauses normally use the same tense. Before a noun use the preposition vor + dative instead: vor der Reise, not bevor der Reise.
compare_en: bevor = before + clause: Bevor wir fahren, … = Before we leave, …. English can say 'before leaving'; German needs a full clause with a subject (bevor wir fahren) or vor + noun (vor der Abfahrt).
title: bevor

pattern: main clause, + um + … + zu + infinitive (at the end)
explain: um … zu + infinitive says why someone does something: its purpose (in order to). Use it when the person doing both actions is the same. um starts the phrase and zu + infinitive go at the end; there is no subject and no conjugated verb. With separable verbs zu goes in the middle: um die Flaschen zurückzubringen.
compare_en: It matches English 'in order to' or just 'to': Ich fahre Rad, um Geld zu sparen = I cycle to save money. But German can't leave out um here.
title: um … zu: purpose

pattern: main clause, + damit + new subject + … + verb (at the end)
explain: damit also gives a purpose (so that), but it starts a full side clause with its own subject, and its verb goes to the end. Use damit when the two parts have different subjects: Ich erkläre es, damit du es verstehst. When both parts have the same subject, um … zu is shorter and sounds better.
compare_en: damit = so that. English 'I'll explain it so that you understand' has the same shape; German just puts the verb at the end: …, damit du es verstehst.
table: Ich fahre Rad, um fit zu bleiben.
Ich fahre Rad, damit die Luft sauberer wird.
title: damit: purpose with a new subject

pattern: Es ist wichtig / Ich habe vor / Ich versuche, + … + zu + infinitive (at the end)
explain: After many adjectives (wichtig, schwer, leicht), nouns (Lust, Zeit, Angst) and verbs (versuchen, vorhaben, anfangen, aufhören, vergessen) the next verb comes as zu + infinitive at the end of the phrase: Es ist wichtig, Wasser zu sparen. The zu part has no subject of its own and is usually separated by a comma. Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen …) never take zu.
compare_en: English uses 'to' in the same places: It's important to save water = Es ist wichtig, Wasser zu sparen. The difference: German puts zu + verb at the very end.
title: Infinitive with zu: Es ist wichtig, … zu …

pattern: sowohl A als auch B · nicht nur A, sondern auch B
explain: These two-part connectors join two things that are both true. sowohl … als auch = both … and; nicht nur … sondern auch = not only … but also, which stresses that the second part is extra or surprising. They can join nouns, adjectives or verb phrases and don't change the word order. Put a comma before sondern.
compare_en: They match English closely: both … and = sowohl … als auch, not only … but also = nicht nur … sondern auch. Careful: 'but' here is sondern, never aber.
title: sowohl … als auch, nicht nur … sondern auch

pattern: weder A noch B (neither … nor) · entweder A oder B (either … or)
explain: weder … noch says that neither of two things is true. It is already negative, so never add nicht or kein: Ich habe weder Zeit noch Geld. entweder … oder offers exactly two choices, one or the other: Wir gehen entweder ins Kino oder ins Theater. Like sowohl … als auch, both pairs can join nouns, adjectives or verbs.
compare_en: weder … noch = neither … nor; entweder … oder = either … or. As in English, don't add a second negative: 'neither … nor' never takes 'not'.
title: weder … noch, entweder … oder

pattern: Je + comparative + subject + … + verb (at the end), desto / umso + comparative + verb + subject + …
explain: je … desto links two things that change together: the more of one, the more of the other. Both parts start with a comparative (mehr, besser, länger). The je part is a side clause, so its verb goes to the end; in the desto part the verb comes straight after desto + comparative. umso means the same as desto.
compare_en: It's English 'the … the …': Je länger ich übe, desto besser spiele ich = The longer I practise, the better I play. German uses two different words, je and desto, with a different word order in each part.
title: je … desto

pattern: masculine 'n-nouns': der Kollege → den / dem / des Kollegen (-n or -en everywhere except the nominative)
explain: A group of masculine nouns adds -n or -en in every case except the nominative singular. They are mostly male people and animals ending in -e (der Kollege, der Kunde, der Junge), words from other languages ending in -ent, -ist, -at (der Student, der Journalist, der Kandidat) and a few others (der Mensch, der Nachbar, der Herr). der Herr takes -n in the singular (dem Herrn) and -en in the plural (die Herren).
compare_en: English has nothing like this. Just remember: with den, dem or des these nouns need their -n: Ich frage den Kollegen, not den Kollege.

en: the way to the town hall

title: n-declension: den Kollegen, dem Herrn

pattern: subject + werden (conjugated) + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: The Futur I is werden + infinitive at the end: Ich werde wählen. When a time word makes the future clear, Germans often just use the present (Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin). Futur I is used for promises, firm plans and predictions (Die Preise werden steigen), and with wohl for a guess about now: Er wird wohl krank sein (he's probably ill).
compare_en: werden + infinitive = will + verb: Ich werde helfen = I will help. Careful: German ich will means 'I want', not 'I will'.
title: Futur I: Ich werde …

pattern: article + Partizip II / Partizip I + adjective ending + noun: das gekochte Ei, das spielende Kind
explain: Participles can stand in front of a noun like adjectives, with the normal adjective endings. A Partizip II (gekocht, gewählt) shows something that has been done to the noun: das gekochte Ei = the egg that has been boiled. A Partizip I (infinitive + d: spielend, steigend) shows something the noun is doing right now: das spielende Kind = the child who is playing. At B1 you only need to recognise them, mostly in newspaper texts.
compare_en: English does the same: the boiled egg, the playing child. German ge-…-t / ge-…-en matches English -ed (done), and -end matches -ing (doing).
table: the repaired street (it has been repaired)
title: Participles as adjectives: das gekochte Ei (recognition)

pattern: als = one event or period in the past · wenn = present / future, or again and again (every time)
explain: Both mean when and send the verb to the end, but they are used differently. Use als for one single event or one period in the past: Als ich 18 war, … Use wenn for the present and the future (Wenn ich fertig bin, …) and for things that happened again and again in the past (Immer wenn wir Oma besuchten, …). wenn can also mean if.
compare_en: English has one word, when. Ask: is it in the past and did it happen only once? Then als; otherwise wenn. Don't confuse either with wann, the question word: Wann kommst du?
title: als or wenn?

pattern: main clause, + während + subject + … + verb (at the end)
explain: As a conjunction, während means while: two things happen at the same time. It starts a side clause, so the verb goes to the end. It can also show a contrast, like English whereas: Lena liebt Sport, während Jonas lieber liest. Don't mix it up with the preposition während + genitive: während des Essens (during the meal).
compare_en: während = while, in both senses (at the same time, and whereas). English 'during' + noun is also während, but then a noun in the genitive follows, not a clause.
title: während: while

pattern: verb + fixed preposition + case: sich bewerben um + accusative, träumen von + dative
explain: Many verbs come with a fixed preposition that you learn together with the verb, because it rarely matches English: sich bewerben um (apply for), träumen von (dream of), sich interessieren für (be interested in), warten auf (wait for). The preposition decides the case. To ask about a thing, use wo(r) + preposition: Wovon träumst du? For a person, use preposition + wen / wem: Von wem träumst du?
compare_en: English verbs have fixed prepositions too, but they seldom match: apply for = sich bewerben um, dream of = träumen von, be interested in = sich interessieren für. Learn each verb with its preposition and case.
title: Verbs with prepositions: sich bewerben um, träumen von

pattern: main clause, + weil / obwohl / damit / nachdem + subject + … + verb (at the end)
explain: These connectors start a side clause and send the conjugated verb to the end. Choose by meaning: weil = reason (because), obwohl = contrast (although), damit = purpose with a new subject (so that), nachdem = one action after another (after). By contrast, deshalb, trotzdem and danach are adverbs: they take position 1 and the verb follows directly. In the exam, a good mix of connectors helps your writing score.
compare_en: The meanings match English because / although / so that / after. The difference is word order: after these German words the verb waits until the end of the clause.
title: Connectors review: weil, obwohl, damit, nachdem

pattern: subject + verb + Te (when) + Ka (why) + Mo (how) + Lo (where) + … (verb part at the end)
explain: In the middle of a German sentence, extra information usually follows the order TeKaMoLo: Temporal (when?), Kausal (why?), Modal (how?), Lokal (where?). So: Ich fahre morgen wegen der Prüfung mit dem Zug nach Berlin. You rarely need all four, but keep the order of those you use. One of them can move to position 1 for emphasis; the verb still stays in position 2.
compare_en: English usually goes the other way round, with place before time: I'm going to Berlin by train tomorrow. German puts time early and place late: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
title: Word order review: TeKaMoLo

pattern: Ich bin der Meinung, dass … · Meiner Meinung nach + verb … · Ich finde, … · Einerseits …, andererseits …
explain: In Schreiben and Sprechen you must give your opinion and back it up. Learn a few fixed phrases with their word order. Ich bin der Meinung, dass … and Ich glaube, dass … send the verb to the end. Meiner Meinung nach takes position 1, so the verb follows straight away: Meiner Meinung nach ist das … Ich finde, … is followed by a normal main clause. To weigh both sides, use einerseits …, andererseits ….
compare_en: Meiner Meinung nach = in my opinion; ich bin der Meinung = I'm of the opinion; einerseits … andererseits = on the one hand … on the other hand. Note: it is ich bin der Meinung, with sein, never ich habe die Meinung.
table: verb right after: Meiner Meinung nach ist …
verb right after each: andererseits gibt es …
title: Exam phrases: giving opinions and reasons
